title: Three at the Arch

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: Sunday is for rest, and Monday is for remembering that you rested.*

Under the arch, the three of them fit. It was the smallest room in Bridgewater, yet somehow it held the most warmth. Hobb sat on his bucket, holding a book open with one massive, mossy finger. He read aloud in a voice that rumbled like distant thunder, though he paused every few pages to hum a tune that went nowhere.

Perrin unrolled a long strip of parchment across the floor. His ink-stained fingers traced the curve of the stone ceiling. Rue stood on a stack of crates, flour on her nose, mixing batter. Half the scones burned, smelling of char and regret. The other half were golden and perfect.

Biscuit, who had followed Rue out of the shop and refused to leave, climbed onto Hobb’s shoulder. The cat sat there, purring, looking exactly like a hat.

"It is a good hat," Hobb said, without looking up from his book.

"It is a cat," Rue corrected.

"He is a good hat," Hobb repeated. Biscuit purred louder.
pages.image: A mossy troll sitting on a bucket inside a stone arch, holding a book, with an enormous orange cat sitting on his shoulder; a small freckled girl mixing batter and a quiet boy drawing on parchment nearby.

pages.text:
Perrin did not stop drawing, but measured the gap between the arch and the water, then the width of the stone, and finally the angle of the light falling across the mud.

He wrote the numbers in his notebook, small and precise, with the careful attention of a child marking the height of a growing plant.

Hobb watched him. "You are measuring the bridge," he said.

"I am measuring the work," Perrin replied. He turned a page, his ink-stained fingers smearing the edge slightly. "You re-seat the loose stones. The river loosens them. You are exactly as fast as the water."

Rue froze, a spoon in her hand, a smudge of batter on her nose. "What?"

"Every night," Hobb said, his leaf-like ears drooping slightly against his spectacles. "I fix what the river takes. It is only a bridge. Somebody has to hold it up."

The proof was sitting right there in the mud and the moss and the neat little numbers in Perrin's book, and it was true. It was the most sensible thing in the whole town. And it was useless, because the town did not want the truth. It wanted a monster.
pages.image: A quiet boy in an oversized wool hat pointing at a notebook filled with numbers, while a large mossy troll looks at the water with a gentle, tired expression; a small girl watches with wide eyes.

pages.text:
Outside the schoolhouse, the air was cold and smelled of wet chalk, and Cedric was waiting by the chestnut tree. Rue had known he was following her for days, a quiet shadow that matched her pace without trying to look like a friend. He did not sneak up this time. He simply stepped out of the shade, his red waistcoat bright against the grey bark, and his eyes were wide and wet.

"The Mayor has a net," Cedric said, his voice thin and cracking. "And a list. A very long list."

Rue felt her knees go weak, as though they had been made of wet bread. "I don't know what you mean."

"Tell me where it is," Cedric whispered, stepping closer until his shoulder brushed the rough bark. "And I'll ask him to spare it."

The word cracked in his mouth. It was not a demand. It was a plea. Rue looked at him, really looked, and saw the fear behind the sneer, the terror of a boy who had built a lie because he was afraid of the truth.

"Nothing in your whole stupid town is as kind as he is," Rue said.
pages.image: A skinny boy in a red waistcoat standing by a tree, looking scared and desperate, facing a small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat who looks angry and sad; a schoolyard in the background.

pages.text:
The words hung in the air, sharp and bright.

The yard went silent. Conversations died in the middle of sentences. Chewing stopped. Heads turned, then turned again, a slow rotation of confusion that felt heavier than the wet chalk smell.

Skye Tanner, who was tall and usually certain, stepped forward. Her long braid swayed against her back. "Who?" she asked.

Cedric’s face went red, then white, and finally a very quiet, terrified grey. He opened his mouth, but no sound came out. He stared at Rue as though she had just bitten him.

Rue realized what she had done exactly as the words left her mouth. It was like seeing a cup slide off the table edge, knowing it would shatter before it even hit the floor. You could hear the crash in your head before the sound reached your ears.

She had not just told them a secret. She had told them a feeling.
pages.image: Skye, a tall girl with a long fair braid, looking shocked; Cedric, a red-faced skinny boy in a red waistcoat, looking horrified; and Rue, a small freckled girl in a mustard raincoat, looking at her own hands in disbelief; a crowd of children in the background

pages.text:
Rue turned and ran.

Her boots slapped against the cobblestones. She ran past the doctor’s house, past the bakery, until her lungs burned and her legs felt like lead. Behind her, the sound of the town changing.

Cedric’s voice rose over the crowd, high and thin. "She knows where he is! She's been going under the bridge!"

Then Skye’s voice, loud and sharp. Then a dozen others. The laughter was gone. The curiosity was gone. In their place was a heavy, ringing sound that started in the center of the town and rolled out to the edges.

The town bell began to ring.

It was not a song. It was a warning. And for the first time in her life, Rue Alder was not running to be useful. She was running because she was alone, and the whole town was coming for her friend.
pages.image: A small girl in a yellow raincoat running away down a cobblestone street, her back to the viewer; in the background, a crowd of children pointing toward the distance, and a large bell tower visible above the rooftops.
